strong.text: You came through with no gaps. You read the patient and the qualifier before choosing, and that habit is what exams reward. Use the review cards to polish anything marked shaky below, and revisit the module in a week to check it holds.

mixed.text: You have a solid base with some real gaps. Where you fell is information: it shows which model to fix, not what you cannot do. Start with the confident errors below, then the gaps, then the shaky areas, and retake the module after reviewing the cards.

weak.text: Several core areas need rebuilding, and that is a clear starting point. Work through the review cards in the order listed, beginning with the traps you fell into confidently. Do the mechanism and signs first, because later management and imaging build on them. Then retake the module.

secure.text: Secure: you read 'most common' as frequency, in general and in pregnancy.

shaky.text: Shaky: you know appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency but wavered, perhaps swayed by graver conditions. Reread the qualifier in each stem.

gap.text: Gap: 'most common' is not holding. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Review the opening card before anything else.

secure.text: Secure: lymphoid hyperplasia for the young, faecolith for adults, and you checked the age.

shaky.text: Shaky: you know both causes but some age matches slipped. Link each to lymphoid tissue, which atrophies with age.

gap.text: Gap: age and obstructing cause are not yet linked. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children, faecolith in adults. Redo the child-versus-adult card.

secure.text: Secure: you order obstruction to pressure to gangrene and explain the shift of pain, with the end artery in mind.

shaky.text: Shaky: the chain mostly holds but a step or the pain shift wobbled. Say the steps aloud: obstruction, pressure, congestion, arterial compromise, gangrene, perforation.

gap.text: Gap: the causal chain is not yet reliable. Obstruction comes first; periumbilical visceral pain shifts to the right iliac fossa when the peritoneum is involved, and the end artery explains rapid gangrene. Review the pathophysiology cards.

secure.text: Secure: you use pain, then vomiting, then fever as a filter against other stories.

shaky.text: Shaky: you know the order but missed using it on a vignette. Ask 'what came first?' on every abdominal story.

gap.text: Gap: symptom order is not yet a tool. Pain first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting first argues against appendicitis. Review the symptom order card.

secure.text: Secure: psoas, obturator and Rovsing each sit on the right manoeuvre and the right position.

shaky.text: Shaky: most signs are right but one pairing slipped. Rehearse the three side by side: Rovsing LIF press, psoas extension, obturator rotation.

gap.text: Gap: the signs and positions are mixed up. Psoas is hip extension with retrocaecal; obturator is internal rotation of the flexed hip with pelvic; Rovsing is left iliac fossa pressure. Start with the sign contrast card.

secure.text: Secure: you know which Alvarado items score 2 and what 7 or more means.

shaky.text: Shaky: the score is partly there. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2; re-add a case from the table to check.

gap.text: Gap: Alvarado is not secure. Two items score 2 (RIF tenderness, leucocytosis), the rest 1, total 10; 7 or more is likely. Rebuild it from the table and practise the arithmetic card.

secure.text: Secure: you chose the first test by patient: ultrasound for children and pregnancy, CECT for adults.

shaky.text: Shaky: the imaging ladder is mostly right but a patient group slipped. Ask who the patient is, then name the rung.

gap.text: Gap: the imaging ladder is not secure. Ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, MRI if inconclusive in pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Review the imaging cards by patient group.

secure.text: Secure: beta-hCG first in women and a look-alike list for each group.

shaky.text: Shaky: you have part of this. Check pregnancy first in reproductive-age women and list one look-alike per age group.

gap.text: Gap: pregnancy testing and look-alikes are not yet automatic. Beta-hCG comes first in women of reproductive age; each group has mimics, such as mittelschmerz or caecal carcinoma. Review the differential card.

secure.text: Secure: you matched surgery or antibiotics-first to the patient, with the qualifiers.

shaky.text: Shaky: you know both options but a qualifier slipped. Antibiotics-first needs CT-proven uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith.

gap.text: Gap: the choice between operating and antibiotics-first is not secure. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is for selected uncomplicated adults. Review the management qualifiers card.

secure.text: Secure: regimen for a mass, drainage for an abscess, selective interval surgery.

shaky.text: Shaky: the ladder mostly holds but one rung slipped. Mass: Ochsner-Sherren; abscess: percutaneous drainage; interval surgery now selective.

gap.text: Gap: mass, abscess and interval surgery are mixed up. A mass is conservative, an abscess drained under imaging, and older patients need colonoscopy or CT before selective interval surgery. Redo the management ladder cards.

secure.text: Secure: you keep disease and operation complications apart and name the ilioinguinal nerve.

shaky.text: Shaky: one list leaked into the other or the nerve wavered. Ask 'disease or knife?' for each complication.

gap.text: Gap: the complication lists are merged. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection, faecal fistula, stump appendicitis, ilioinguinal injury. Rebuild both lists and review the nerve card.

secure.text: Secure: carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour and you know the 2 cm rule.

shaky.text: Shaky: you recall the tumour but the size rule wobbled. Under 2 cm at the tip, appendicectomy; larger or base involvement, hemicolectomy.

gap.text: Gap: the tumour and its size rule are not yet held. Carcinoid is commonest; under 2 cm appendicectomy usually suffices, larger needs right hemicolectomy. Review the tumour card.

avoided.text: Psoas and obturator sit on the right movements for you. Keep rehearsing by the movement.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the two hip manoeuvres at first, then corrected. Extension of the hip is psoas; internal rotation of the flexed hip is obturator. Under exam pressure the names can flip again, so say the movement first, then the name.

fell_open.text: You swapped the psoas and obturator manoeuvres. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Psoas is pain on hip extension; obturator is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip. Say the movement first, then the name. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You link signs to appendix positions through the organ touched. That is the durable way.

fell_recovered.text: You first attached the signs to the wrong positions, then rebuilt them. Psoas goes with retrocaecal, obturator and right rectal tenderness with pelvic. When rushed, ask which organ the appendix is touching.

fell_open.text: You tied a sign to the wrong appendix position. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Psoas goes with a retrocaecal appendix on the muscle; obturator and right rectal tenderness go with a pelvic appendix. Ask which organ the appendix touches. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: Rovsing's direction is secure for you: press left, hurts right.

fell_recovered.text: You reversed Rovsing's sign at first, then fixed it. Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right. Under time pressure, narrate it as 'press here, hurts there' before choosing.

fell_open.text: You ran Rovsing's sign backwards. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Rovsing's sign is pressure in the left iliac fossa causing pain in the right. Say it as 'press here, hurts there'. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You trace appendicitis cause to effect: blockage first, then pain moving from umbilicus to right iliac fossa.

fell_recovered.text: You started from the end picture, then corrected the chain. Obstruction raises pressure, congestion and arterial compromise follow, then gangrene and perforation; pain starts periumbilical and shifts. In a cold stem, say the steps aloud in order.

fell_open.text: You reversed the pain pathway or the causal chain. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. The chain starts with obstruction and rising pressure; early pain is periumbilical and shifts when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed. Say the steps in order. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You use symptom order as a clue: pain first, then vomiting, then fever.

fell_recovered.text: You first put vomiting ahead of pain, then corrected. In appendicitis pain comes first; vomiting first points to gastroenteritis. Keep pain-first as a quick filter when a story seems off.

fell_open.text: You put vomiting ahead of pain. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. In appendicitis pain comes first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting first argues against it. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: The 2-point Alvarado items and the cut-off are secure for you.

fell_recovered.text: You misplaced the 2-point items or the meaning of the cut-off, then rebuilt them. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2, out of 10; 7 or more is likely, not proof. Re-add from the table when numbers appear in an exam.

fell_open.text: You misweighted the Alvarado score or read it as a diagnosis. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Only right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2, out of 10; 7 or more makes appendicitis likely, not certain. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You know ultrasound is first-line, not final, in adults. Good.

fell_recovered.text: You first took a negative ultrasound as the end of the work-up, then corrected. In an adult, an unhelpful scan leads on to contrast CT, which is more accurate. Keep that next-step reflex.

fell_open.text: You treated a negative ultrasound as excluding appendicitis in an adult. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. An unhelpful scan does not end the work-up; contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test in adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You read the patient before choosing the test. Children and pregnancy change the first scan.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave CT to a child or pregnant patient, then corrected. Ultrasound comes first in both; CT is the adult answer. When a stem names age or pregnancy, circle it before choosing.

fell_open.text: You chose CT first for a child or pregnant patient. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Ultrasound is first in children and pregnancy; contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults. Check who the patient is. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: Your pregnancy ladder runs ultrasound, then MRI. Right order.

fell_recovered.text: You first put MRI at the top of the pregnancy ladder, then corrected. Ultrasound is the first rung; MRI without gadolinium is used when ultrasound is inconclusive. Remember accuracy is not the only criterion for a first test.

fell_open.text: You put MRI first in pregnancy. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Graded-compression ultrasound is the first rung; MRI without gadolinium is the second, when ultrasound is inconclusive. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You answer 'investigation of choice' by reading the qualifier. Good exam habit.

fell_recovered.text: You first answered from the older ultrasound key, then corrected. Older keys favoured ultrasound; current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Keep both as a pair.

fell_open.text: You answered from the old ultrasound key for an adult. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, and contrast-enhanced CT as the most accurate test in adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: Beta-hCG comes first in your plan for women of reproductive age.

fell_recovered.text: You first skipped or delayed the pregnancy test, then corrected. Ectopic pregnancy changes both imaging and surgery, so test first. Under pressure, the favoured diagnosis can crowd this step out.

fell_open.text: You skipped or delayed the pregnancy test. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. In any woman of reproductive age, beta-hCG comes before imaging or theatre, because ectopic pregnancy changes the plan. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You read 'most common' as frequency, not severity.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked a more dramatic emergency, then corrected. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Read the qualifier word before the options.

fell_open.text: You picked a more dramatic condition as the most common. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Most common means most frequent: appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, and carcinoid the commonest appendix tumour. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You build a differential by age and sex rather than defaulting to appendicitis.

fell_recovered.text: You first called a look-alike appendicitis, then corrected. Mittelschmerz fits young women with brief mid-cycle pain; caecal carcinoma fits an older man with a mass and anaemia. Keep generating look-alikes for each group.

fell_open.text: You assumed right iliac fossa pain always means appendicitis. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Each group has look-alikes, such as mesenteric lymphadenitis in children, mittelschmerz and PID in women, and caecal carcinoma in older patients. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You check the age before naming the cause of obstruction.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave the cause for the wrong age group, then corrected. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults. Tie it to lymphoid tissue that atrophies with age.

fell_open.text: You ignored the age when naming the cause of the block. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults, as lymphoid tissue atrophies with age. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You keep disease complications and operation complications apart.

fell_recovered.text: You first merged the two complication lists, then rebuilt them. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection (commonest), faecal fistula, stump appendicitis. Ask 'disease or knife?' for each item.

fell_open.text: You merged complications of the disease with those of the operation. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Pylephlebitis, mass and abscess come from the disease; wound infection, faecal fistula and stump appendicitis follow surgery. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: The gridiron incision and the ilioinguinal nerve are paired in your memory.

fell_recovered.text: You first named a neighbouring nerve, then corrected. The ilioinguinal nerve is injured by a gridiron incision, leading to right inguinal hernia. Draw it on the site if it wobbles.

fell_open.text: You named a neighbouring nerve instead of the one a gridiron incision endangers. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. The ilioinguinal nerve is the one at risk, leading to a right inguinal hernia. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You separate the exam key from practice: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, with antibiotics-first for selected patients.

fell_recovered.text: You first held that surgery is the only option, then corrected. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is accepted for selected uncomplicated cases. Give both in an exam answer.

fell_open.text: You took 'treatment of choice' to mean the only treatment. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, but antibiotics-first is accepted for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You check the qualifiers before offering antibiotics-first.

fell_recovered.text: You first offered antibiotics-first too widely, then corrected. It suits CT-proven uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith; an appendicolith predicts failure. Keep the three conditions together.

fell_open.text: You offered antibiotics-first without its conditions. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. It suits selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith; an appendicolith predicts failure. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You give the old key and the modern view of interval surgery.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied interval surgery to everyone, then corrected. Traditionally it was done at 6-8 weeks; now it is selective, with colonoscopy or CT in older patients to exclude caecal carcinoma. Under pressure, remember the older-patient work-up.

fell_open.text: You applied interval appendicectomy routinely after a mass. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. It is now selective, and patients over about 40 need colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

avoided.text: You pick the right first step for mass and for abscess.

fell_recovered.text: You first chose surgery up front, then corrected. A mass gets the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess gets image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics. Know when the regimen stops.

fell_open.text: You went straight to surgery or open drainage. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. A stable mass gets the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess gets image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

E1.text: You tend to swap names between look-alike items that share a category. Next time, anchor each name to its defining movement or feature and say it before choosing.

E2.text: You tend to merge two lists that live in the same chapter. Before picking, ask which list the item belongs to, and rebuild each list from its logic.

E3.text: You tend to run a sequence or direction backwards, starting from the end picture. Narrate the process cause first, 'press here, hurts there' or 'blockage, then pressure'.

E4.text: You tend to read a qualifier or a pattern too narrowly: 'most common' as 'most serious', or a classic picture as the only one. Underline the qualifier, then ask what else fits.

E5.text: You tend to answer from a remembered past-paper key without checking current practice. In such stems, give the old key and the modern view as a pair.

E6.text: You tend to remember numbers by how important they feel rather than by the table. Rebuild scores from their items and re-add them before choosing.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier, such as age, pregnancy or appendicolith, and apply a general answer. Circle the patient detail before looking at the options.

E8.text: You tend to treat the first or most accurate test as the whole pathway. Think in rungs: what comes first, what comes after an unhelpful result.

E9.text: You tend to start with the favoured diagnosis and skip the step that comes first. Ask 'what first, and why' before committing to a plan.

E10.text: You tend to pair items correctly in form but attach them to the wrong partner. Rebuild the pair from the anatomy it depends on rather than recalling the pair.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those are the costly ones, because you stop checking. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or the rule you are relying on; if you cannot, tap Guessing.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on three or more answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, give a one-line reason before answering, and tap Sure when you can.

calibrated.text: Your Sure taps matched your answers. That is a useful signal: trust Sure when you can state a reason, and treat Guessing as a prompt to review that card.

hints_heavy.text: You opened hints three or more times. Using them is fine early on; the aim is to need them less. Pick two objectives you hinted on and try the matching cards cold before your next session.

hints_none.text: You used no hints and still fell into traps. Hints on the questions you were unsure about would have flagged the qualifier. Next time, open one before a stem with an age, a pregnancy or an exam-key flavour.

hinted_only.text: On at least one objective you got it right only after a hint. That counts as not yet secure. Try that objective's review card with no help in a day or so.

fast_lane.text: You took a fast lane after a correct, confident answer and skipped some teaching. Check the objectives listed as shaky or gap: if the skipped topic appears there, review its card.

gap.text: Review the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky. Do two or three per sitting, answer before reading, then retake this module in about a week to see which models have changed.

clear.text: No gaps showed. Keep the schedule of review cards at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days and practise mixed-age imaging and management stems to stay sharp.
